lessonTitle: Minerals and Nutritional Assessment: Iron, Calcium, Iodine, Zinc and BMI

blocks.text: A 14-year-old girl who eats little meat and has heavy periods complains of constant tiredness and breathlessness on stairs. Her skin is pale and her blood film shows small, pale red cells. The body has no way to excrete excess iron and little way to make up a shortfall, so understanding how iron is absorbed, carried and stored explains why this common deficiency arises and how it is recognised.

blocks.markdown: **The idea.** Minerals are inorganic elements the body cannot synthesise. Some are needed in large amounts (calcium) and others in traces (iron, iodine, zinc), but each has a defined role. This unit covers iron in detail, then the physiological importance of calcium, iodine and zinc, and finally how body mass index (BMI) is used to screen nutritional status.

blocks.title: Iron handling
blocks.text: Dietary iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, carried in plasma bound to transferrin, and stored inside cells as ferritin. There is no regulated excretory pathway for iron, so the body controls iron balance by regulating absorption, chiefly through the hormone hepcidin.

blocks.markdown: **Absorption.** Food contains **haem iron** (from meat, absorbed efficiently as intact haem) and **non-haem iron** (from plants and supplements, mostly as ferric Fe3+). Non-haem iron must be reduced to ferrous Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome B on the enterocyte surface (a step helped by **vitamin C**) before the divalent metal transporter DMT1 takes it up. **Phytates, tannins (tea) and calcium** reduce absorption. Inside the enterocyte iron is either stored as ferritin (and lost when the cell is shed) or exported across the basolateral membrane by **ferroportin**, the only known cellular iron exporter. It is oxidised back to Fe3+ by hephaestin to be loaded on transferrin.

**Transport, storage and control.** **Transferrin** carries up to two Fe3+ ions and delivers them to cells (such as erythroid precursors) through the transferrin receptor. **Ferritin** is the intracellular storage protein (in liver, spleen and marrow); a small amount leaks into plasma and, in the absence of inflammation, the serum ferritin reflects iron stores. **Hepcidin**, made by the liver, binds ferroportin and causes its degradation, so iron is trapped in enterocytes and macrophages and less enters plasma. Hepcidin rises with iron overload and inflammation and falls in iron deficiency and increased erythropoiesis.

blocks.caption: Interpreting iron studies. Reference intervals differ between laboratories; check local ranges.

blocks.title: Transferrin saturation
blocks.prompt: A patient has serum iron 20 micromol per litre and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) 50 micromol per litre. Calculate the transferrin saturation.

steps.text: TIBC measures the total capacity of transferrin to bind iron; serum iron measures how much is currently bound.
Transferrin saturation = serum iron divided by TIBC, multiplied by 100%.

blocks.answer: 40%. Low values suggest iron deficiency and high values suggest overload; the cut-offs depend on the laboratory and the clinical question.

blocks.markdown: **Calcium.** About 99% of body calcium is in bone and teeth as hydroxyapatite, which acts as a reservoir. The remaining 1% has critical roles: **muscle contraction** (including cardiac), **neurotransmitter release**, **blood clotting** (factor binding to phospholipid), enzyme activation and intracellular signalling. Plasma calcium is roughly half **ionised** (the physiologically active fraction), with most of the rest bound to albumin, so low albumin lowers total calcium without lowering ionised calcium. Plasma calcium is tightly controlled by parathyroid hormone (PTH), active vitamin D and calcitonin; low ionised calcium causes neuromuscular irritability (tingling, tetany, cramps), while excess causes weakness, constipation and kidney stones.

**Iodine.** Iodine is an essential component of the thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4, four iodine atoms) and triiodothyronine (T3, three). The thyroid takes up iodide, and thyroid peroxidase iodinates tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin. Deficiency lowers hormone output, raising TSH, which causes thyroid enlargement (**goitre**) and hypothyroidism; in pregnancy it causes impaired fetal brain development (cretinism). **Zinc** is a cofactor for over a hundred enzymes (for example carbonic anhydrase, alcohol dehydrogenase and Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase), forms structural zinc finger motifs in transcription factors, and is needed for wound healing, immunity and taste. Deficiency causes a skin rash around the mouth and extremities, diarrhoea, hair loss, poor wound healing, impaired taste and growth failure; the inherited form is acrodermatitis enteropathica.

rows: Haem in haemoglobin and myoglobin; cytochromes
Tetany, cramps, osteoporosis in long-term deficiency
Enzyme cofactor, zinc fingers, wound healing
Dermatitis, diarrhoea, hair loss, poor wound healing, loss of taste

blocks.title: Calculating and interpreting BMI
blocks.prompt: A man has mass 70 kg and height 1.75 m. Calculate his BMI and classify it using the WHO adult categories (below 18.5 underweight; 18.5 to 24.9 normal; 25.0 to 29.9 overweight; 30.0 and above obese).
blocks.answer: BMI 22.9 kg per square metre, in the normal range. BMI is a screening tool: it does not distinguish muscle from fat or show fat distribution, and cut-offs may differ in some ethnic groups, so waist circumference and clinical assessment complement it.

blocks.title: Energy balance and BMI
blocks.text: Body weight is stable when energy intake equals energy expenditure. Sustained positive balance raises BMI through fat storage; sustained negative balance lowers it through loss of fat and lean mass. BMI therefore screens for risk, but a diagnosis of malnutrition needs dietary history, examination and biochemical tests.

blocks.title: Ferritin and inflammation
blocks.text: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein. In infection or inflammation it may be normal or high even when iron stores are low, so interpret it with transferrin saturation and inflammatory markers.

points: Iron is absorbed as haem or reduced non-haem iron, exported by ferroportin, carried by transferrin and stored as ferritin, with absorption controlled by hepcidin.
Calcium supports bone, muscle contraction and clotting; iodine is needed for thyroid hormones; zinc is an enzyme cofactor needed for wound healing and immunity.
BMI is mass in kilograms divided by height in metres squared and is interpreted using WHO categories, with recognised limitations.

questions.stem: Which protein exports iron from intestinal enterocytes into the plasma?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ferroportin is the basolateral iron exporter.
distractorRationale.b: The transferrin receptor takes up transferrin-bound iron into cells.
distractorRationale.c: Ferritin stores iron inside cells and does not export it.
distractorRationale.d: DMT1 imports ferrous iron across the apical membrane into the enterocyte.

questions.explanation: Iron enters enterocytes through DMT1 and leaves across the basolateral membrane through ferroportin, after which it is oxidised and loaded on transferrin. Hepcidin controls iron absorption by degrading ferroportin.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has anaemia, low serum iron, a normal serum ferritin and a raised plasma hepcidin. How does the raised hepcidin explain the low serum iron?

options.text: Hepcidin degrades ferroportin, trapping iron in enterocytes and macrophages and lowering plasma iron
Hepcidin blocks the transferrin receptor on red cell precursors
Hepcidin increases iron excretion in the urine

questions.correctOptionText: Hepcidin degrades ferroportin, trapping iron in enterocytes and macrophages and lowering plasma iron

distractorRationale.a: Correct: hepcidin causes degradation of ferroportin, reducing iron entry into plasma.
distractorRationale.b: Hepcidin acts on ferroportin, not on the transferrin receptor.
distractorRationale.c: There is no significant regulated iron excretion; hepcidin acts on release from cells.
distractorRationale.d: Ferritin is the storage form and is not destroyed by hepcidin; it is typically normal or raised in inflammation.

questions.explanation: Inflammation raises hepcidin, which causes ferroportin to be internalised and degraded. Iron is therefore retained in enterocytes and macrophages, so plasma iron falls while stores (ferritin) stay normal or rise.

questions.stem: Which dietary factor increases the absorption of non-haem iron?

options.text: Vitamin C, which reduces ferric iron to ferrous iron

questions.correctOptionText: Vitamin C, which reduces ferric iron to ferrous iron

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ascorbate reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+, the form taken up by DMT1.
distractorRationale.b: Tannins bind iron and reduce absorption.
distractorRationale.c: Phytates chelate iron and inhibit absorption.

questions.explanation: Non-haem iron is mainly ferric and must be reduced to ferrous iron before DMT1 can transport it. Vitamin C helps this reduction, whereas tannins, phytates and calcium reduce absorption.

questions.stem: A woman living in a mountain region far from the sea has a visibly enlarged neck with a diffuse thyroid swelling and a raised TSH. Which dietary mineral deficiency is the most likely cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: iodine is needed for thyroid hormone, and deficiency causes goitre through raised TSH.
distractorRationale.b: Zinc deficiency causes skin changes, diarrhoea and poor wound healing, not goitre.
distractorRationale.c: Iron deficiency causes anaemia, not diffuse thyroid enlargement.
distractorRationale.d: Calcium deficiency causes tetany and bone loss, not goitre.

questions.explanation: Without enough iodine the thyroid cannot make T3 and T4, so negative feedback is lost, TSH rises and the gland enlarges as a goitre. Iodine-poor soils inland are a classic cause.

questions.stem: An 8-month-old, recently weaned from breast milk, has a red scaly rash around the mouth and on the hands and feet, along with diarrhoea and thinning hair. Which mineral deficiency is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: periorificial and acral dermatitis, diarrhoea and alopecia are characteristic of zinc deficiency (including acrodermatitis enteropathica).
distractorRationale.b: Iodine deficiency would cause goitre and hypothyroidism.
distractorRationale.c: Iron deficiency presents with pallor and fatigue, not this rash.
distractorRationale.d: Calcium deficiency causes tetany or rickets-type problems.

questions.explanation: Zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes and for zinc finger proteins, so rapidly dividing tissues such as skin and gut are affected first. The rash with diarrhoea and hair loss is typical, and breast milk zinc is well absorbed, so symptoms often appear on weaning in the inherited form.

questions.stem: True or false: the physiologically active fraction of plasma calcium is the ionised (free) calcium.
questions.explanation: Only the ionised fraction takes part in physiological processes such as muscle contraction and neuromuscular excitability. Calcium bound to albumin is inactive, which is why changes in albumin alter total but not ionised calcium.

questions.stem: A man has a body mass of 95 kg and a height of 1.80 m. Calculate his body mass index.
questions.explanation: Height squared is 1.80 x 1.80 = 3.24 square metres, so BMI = 95 / 3.24 = 29.3 kg per square metre. This falls in the WHO overweight category (25.0 to 29.9), just below the obesity threshold.

questions.stem: A patient has serum iron 9 micromol per litre and total iron-binding capacity 60 micromol per litre. Calculate the transferrin saturation as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Transferrin saturation = serum iron divided by total iron-binding capacity, multiplied by 100: 9 / 60 x 100 = 15 percent. A low saturation together with a high binding capacity is the pattern seen in iron deficiency (interpret against local reference intervals).

questions.stem: Describe how dietary iron is absorbed, transported and stored, and explain how hepcidin regulates iron balance.
markingGuide: Haem iron is absorbed as haem; non-haem iron is reduced to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome B (helped by vitamin C) and enters via DMT1 in the duodenum
Enhancers (vitamin C) and inhibitors (phytate, tannins, calcium) of non-haem iron absorption
Export across basolateral membrane by ferroportin; oxidation to Fe3+ by hephaestin
Transport in plasma bound to transferrin (up to two Fe3+) and uptake by transferrin receptor
Storage as ferritin in liver, spleen and marrow; serum ferritin reflects stores
Hepcidin from liver degrades ferroportin, reducing absorption and iron release from macrophages; raised in inflammation and overload, lowered in deficiency
No regulated excretion, so control is by absorption
questions.explanation: Iron balance is controlled at the point of absorption because the body cannot excrete it. Hepcidin acts as the master regulator by degrading ferroportin, the single route by which iron enters plasma.

questions.stem: Explain how body mass index is calculated and interpreted in nutritional assessment, giving the WHO adult categories, and discuss two limitations of BMI.
markingGuide: BMI = mass in kg divided by height in metres squared
WHO categories: below 18.5 underweight; 18.5 to 24.9 normal; 25.0 to 29.9 overweight; 30.0 and above obese
Used as a screening tool for nutritional risk and weight-related disease risk
Limitation: does not distinguish fat from lean mass (muscular individuals may be classed overweight)
Limitation: does not show fat distribution (central adiposity); cut-offs may differ by ethnic group and age; may be misleading in oedema
Should be combined with history, examination, waist circumference and biochemical tests
questions.explanation: BMI normalises weight for height so that populations can be compared with a single number. Because it is a ratio rather than a body composition measure, it is a screening tool and must be interpreted alongside clinical findings.
